Gradients and Hessians with RTMB

Source: vignettes/articles/rtmb.qmd

RTMB (Kristensen, 2026) differentiates a function written in R. RTMB::MakeADFun() runs the function once on RTMB’s own type of number and records every operation. obj$fn, obj$gr and obj$he then replay that record, the tape, to give the value, the exact gradient and the exact Hessian at any parameter value. RTMB is the R interface to TMB (Kristensen et al., 2016), whose models are written as C++ templates. RTMB needs neither C++ nor a compiler.

This article writes the structural equation model of Speeding up with Rcpp, with 39 parameters, for RTMB, and compares the fit with the R and C++ fits of that article, for speed and for accuracy, with and without RTMB’s Hessian. The model, its parameterisation and its priors are described there.

library(inlavanilla)
data(PoliticalDemocracy, package = "lavaan")

The data, the layout of the parameters, the starting values and the R log-posterior logpost_r() are those of the Rcpp article, and so are the C++ log-posterior logpost_cpp() and its gradient grad_cpp(), written by hand from the closed-form gradient of a structural equation model (Neudecker & Satorra, 1991). Expand the code to see them.

R code from the Rcpp article
ov <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", paste0("y", 1:8))
Y <- as.matrix(PoliticalDemocracy[, ov])

cov_pairs <- rbind(
  c("y1", "y5"),
  c("y2", "y4"),
  c("y2", "y6"),
  c("y3", "y7"),
  c("y4", "y8"),
  c("y6", "y8")
)

lambda_fixed <- matrix(0, 11, 3)
lambda_fixed[cbind(c(1, 4, 8), 1:3)] <- 1
lambda_at <- cbind(c(2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11), rep(1:3, c(2, 3, 3)))
lambda_par <- c(12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 14, 15, 16)
beta_at <- cbind(c(2, 3, 3), c(1, 1, 2))
cov_at <- matrix(match(cov_pairs, ov), ncol = 2)

implied_cov <- function(theta) {
  Lambda <- lambda_fixed
  Lambda[lambda_at] <- theta[lambda_par]
  B <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
  B[beta_at] <- theta[17:19]
  psi <- exp(theta[20:22])
  v <- exp(theta[23:33])
  Theta <- diag(v)
  Theta[cov_at] <- tanh(theta[34:39]) * sqrt(v[cov_at[, 1]] * v[cov_at[, 2]])
  Theta[cov_at[, 2:1]] <- Theta[cov_at]
  LA <- Lambda %*% solve(diag(3) - B)
  LA %*% (psi * t(LA)) + Theta # LA Psi LA' + Theta
}

loglik_r <- function(theta, Y) {
  Sigma <- implied_cov(theta)
  R <- tryCatch(chol(Sigma), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(R)) {
    return(rep(-Inf, nrow(Y))) # Sigma is not positive definite
  }
  Z <- backsolve(R, t(Y) - theta[1:11], transpose = TRUE)
  -0.5 * ncol(Y) * log(2 * pi) - sum(log(diag(R))) - 0.5 * colSums(Z^2)
}

logprior_r <- function(theta) {
  logv <- theta[20:33]
  sd <- exp(logv / 2)
  rho <- tanh(theta[34:39])
  sum(dnorm(theta[1:11], 0, 32, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(dnorm(theta[12:19], 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(dgamma(sd, shape = 1, rate = 0.5, log = TRUE) + log(sd / 2)) +
    sum(dbeta((rho + 1) / 2, 1, 1, log = TRUE) - log(2) + log1p(-rho^2))
}

logpost_r <- function(theta, Y) {
  sum(loglik_r(theta, Y)) + logprior_r(theta)
}

init <- c(
  colMeans(Y),
  rep(1, 5),
  rep(0, 3),
  rep(0, 3),
  log(apply(Y, 2, var) / 2),
  rep(0, 6)
)
names(init) <- c(
  paste0("nu_", ov),
  c("lam_x2", "lam_x3", "a", "b", "c"),
  c("beta_dem60_ind60", "beta_dem65_ind60", "beta_dem65_dem60"),
  paste0("logv_", c("ind60", "dem60", "dem65")),
  paste0("logv_", ov),
  paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2])
)
C++ code from the Rcpp article
Rcpp::sourceCpp(
  code = r"(
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppEigen)]]
#include <RcppEigen.h>

using Eigen::Map;
using Eigen::MatrixXd;
using Eigen::VectorXd;

// theta: intercepts 0-10, loadings 11-15, regressions 16-18, latent log
// variances 19-21, residual log variances 22-32, residual correlations
// (atanh scale) 33-38. Indicators in the order x1, x2, x3, y1, ..., y8.

// Free loadings: row and column of Lambda, and the element of theta
const int lambda_row[8] = {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10};
const int lambda_col[8] = {0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2};
const int lambda_par[8] = {11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 13, 14, 15};
// Regressions: dem60 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ dem60
const int beta_row[3] = {1, 2, 2};
const int beta_col[3] = {0, 0, 1};
// Residual covariances: y1-y5, y2-y4, y2-y6, y3-y7, y4-y8, y6-y8
const int cov_i[6] = {3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8};
const int cov_j[6] = {7, 6, 8, 9, 10, 10};

struct Sem {
  VectorXd nu, psi, v, rho;
  MatrixXd Lambda, A, M, Theta, Sigma;  // A = (I - B)^-1, M = A Psi A'
};

Sem sem_matrices(const VectorXd& theta) {
  Sem s;
  s.nu = theta.head(11);
  s.Lambda = MatrixXd::Zero(11, 3);
  s.Lambda(0, 0) = s.Lambda(3, 1) = s.Lambda(7, 2) = 1;
  for (int k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
    s.Lambda(lambda_row[k], lambda_col[k]) = theta[lambda_par[k]];
  }
  MatrixXd B = MatrixXd::Zero(3, 3);
  for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) B(beta_row[k], beta_col[k]) = theta[16 + k];
  s.A = (MatrixXd::Identity(3, 3) - B).inverse();
  s.psi = theta.segment(19, 3).array().exp();
  s.v = theta.segment(22, 11).array().exp();
  s.rho = theta.segment(33, 6).array().tanh();
  s.Theta = s.v.asDiagonal();
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    int i = cov_i[k], j = cov_j[k];
    s.Theta(i, j) = s.Theta(j, i) = s.rho[k] * std::sqrt(s.v[i] * s.v[j]);
  }
  s.M = s.A * s.psi.asDiagonal() * s.A.transpose();
  s.Sigma = s.Lambda * s.M * s.Lambda.transpose() + s.Theta;
  return s;
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
VectorXd loglik_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta, const Map<MatrixXd> Y) {
  Sem s = sem_matrices(theta);
  Eigen::LLT<MatrixXd> llt(s.Sigma);
  if (llt.info() != Eigen::Success) {  // Sigma is not positive definite
    return VectorXd::Constant(Y.rows(), R_NegInf);
  }
  MatrixXd D = Y.rowwise() - s.nu.transpose();
  MatrixXd Z = llt.matrixL().solve(D.transpose());
  // matrixLLT() holds L, whose diagonal gives half the log-determinant
  double half_logdet = llt.matrixLLT().diagonal().array().log().sum();
  double c = -0.5 * Y.cols() * std::log(2 * M_PI) - half_logdet;
  return (c - 0.5 * Z.colwise().squaredNorm().array()).matrix().transpose();
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
double logprior_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta) {
  double lp = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 11; i++) lp += R::dnorm(theta[i], 0, 32, true);
  for (int i = 11; i < 19; i++) lp += R::dnorm(theta[i], 0, 10, true);
  for (int i = 19; i < 33; i++) {
    double sd = std::exp(theta[i] / 2);
    // R::dgamma() takes the scale, 1 / rate
    lp += R::dgamma(sd, 1, 1 / 0.5, true) + std::log(sd / 2);
  }
  for (int i = 33; i < 39; i++) {
    double rho = std::tanh(theta[i]);
    lp += R::dbeta((rho + 1) / 2, 1, 1, true) - std::log(2.0) +
      std::log1p(-rho * rho);
  }
  return lp;
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
double logpost_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta, const Map<MatrixXd> Y) {
  return loglik_cpp(theta, Y).sum() + logprior_cpp(theta);
}
// Gradient of logpost_cpp() with respect to theta
// [[Rcpp::export]]
VectorXd grad_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta, const Map<MatrixXd> Y) {
  Sem s = sem_matrices(theta);
  Eigen::LLT<MatrixXd> llt(s.Sigma);
  if (llt.info() != Eigen::Success) return VectorXd::Constant(39, NA_REAL);
  VectorXd g = VectorXd::Zero(39);

  // Log-likelihood, through G = d loglik / d Sigma
  int n = Y.rows();
  MatrixXd Omega = llt.solve(MatrixXd::Identity(11, 11));
  MatrixXd OD = Omega * (Y.rowwise() - s.nu.transpose()).transpose();
  MatrixXd G = 0.5 * (OD * OD.transpose() - n * Omega);

  g.head(11) = OD.rowwise().sum();
  MatrixXd dLambda = 2 * G * s.Lambda * s.M;
  for (int k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
    g[lambda_par[k]] += dLambda(lambda_row[k], lambda_col[k]);
  }
  MatrixXd LGL = s.Lambda.transpose() * G * s.Lambda;
  MatrixXd dB = 2 * s.A.transpose() * LGL * s.M;
  for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) g[16 + k] = dB(beta_row[k], beta_col[k]);
  MatrixXd dPsi = s.A.transpose() * LGL * s.A;
  for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) g[19 + k] = dPsi(k, k) * s.psi[k];
  for (int i = 0; i < 11; i++) g[22 + i] = G(i, i) * s.v[i];
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    int i = cov_i[k], j = cov_j[k];
    g[22 + i] += G(i, j) * s.Theta(i, j);
    g[22 + j] += G(i, j) * s.Theta(i, j);
    g[33 + k] = 2 * G(i, j) * (1 - s.rho[k] * s.rho[k]) *
      std::sqrt(s.v[i] * s.v[j]);
  }

  // Log-prior, with the Jacobians
  for (int i = 0; i < 11; i++) g[i] -= theta[i] / (32.0 * 32.0);
  for (int i = 11; i < 19; i++) g[i] -= theta[i] / (10.0 * 10.0);
  for (int i = 19; i < 33; i++) g[i] += 0.5 - std::exp(theta[i] / 2) / 4;
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) g[33 + k] -= 2 * s.rho[k];
  return g;
}
)"
)

The log-posterior in RTMB

logpost_rtmb() is logpost_r() with three changes:

  • The densities, diag() and solve() are RTMB’s, which also take its numbers. We call them with RTMB:: rather than attaching the package: library(RTMB) masks the base and stats functions of the same names, and slows ordinary R code that calls them, logpost_r() among it.
  • "[<-" <- RTMB::ADoverload("[<-") lets RTMB’s numbers be assigned into the ordinary matrices \(\Lambda\), \(B\) and \(\Theta\).
  • RTMB::dmvnorm() replaces the Cholesky factor and its tryCatch(). The tape keeps the path taken when it was recorded, so a branch on the parameters, such as returning -Inf when \(\Sigma\) is not positive definite, cannot be recorded. Where \(\Sigma\) is not positive definite the tape gives NaN, which inla_vanilla() treats as -Inf.
logpost_rtmb <- function(theta, Y) {
  "[<-" <- RTMB::ADoverload("[<-")
  Lambda <- lambda_fixed
  Lambda[lambda_at] <- theta[lambda_par]
  B <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
  B[beta_at] <- theta[17:19]
  psi <- exp(theta[20:22])
  v <- exp(theta[23:33])
  Theta <- RTMB::diag(v)
  Theta[cov_at] <- tanh(theta[34:39]) * sqrt(v[cov_at[, 1]] * v[cov_at[, 2]])
  Theta[cov_at[, 2:1]] <- Theta[cov_at]
  LA <- Lambda %*% RTMB::solve(diag(3) - B)
  Sigma <- LA %*% (psi * t(LA)) + Theta
  loglik <- RTMB::dmvnorm(t(t(Y) - theta[1:11]), Sigma = Sigma, log = TRUE)

  sd <- exp(theta[20:33] / 2)
  rho <- tanh(theta[34:39])
  logprior <- sum(RTMB::dnorm(theta[1:11], 0, 32, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(RTMB::dnorm(theta[12:19], 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(RTMB::dgamma(sd, shape = 1, rate = 0.5, log = TRUE) + log(sd / 2)) +
    sum(RTMB::dbeta((rho + 1) / 2, 1, 1, log = TRUE) - log(2) + log1p(-rho^2))
  sum(loglik) + logprior
}

RTMB::MakeADFun() takes a function of a list of parameters. TMB’s objectives are usually negative log-likelihoods, to be minimised, but the sign matters only when random effects are integrated out. There are none here, so the function returns the log-posterior itself, and obj$fn, obj$gr and obj$he go to inla_vanilla() as they are.

obj <- RTMB::MakeADFun(
  function(p) logpost_rtmb(p$theta, Y),
  list(theta = unname(init)),
  silent = TRUE
)

obj$he works out the Hessian from the recorded function at each call. A Hessian tape is faster: RTMB::MakeTape() records the function, which here takes the parameter vector itself, $jacfun() records the computation of its gradient, and a second $jacfun() that of its Hessian, so that each call replays the Hessian’s own computation.

hess_tape <- RTMB::MakeTape(
  function(theta) logpost_rtmb(theta, Y),
  unname(init)
)$jacfun()$jacfun()

At 200 points around the starting values, the value matches the R log-posterior, and the gradient the hand-written one, to rounding error:

set.seed(1)
points <- replicate(200, init + rnorm(39, sd = 0.05), simplify = FALSE)
value_error <- function(th) abs(obj$fn(th) - logpost_r(th, Y))
grad_error <- function(th) max(abs(obj$gr(th) - grad_cpp(th, Y)))
c(
  value = max(vapply(points, value_error, 0)),
  gradient = max(vapply(points, grad_error, 0))
)
#>        value     gradient 
#> 1.364242e-12 1.136868e-13

Speed

The time per call, in microseconds, over the same 200 points. (Repeated calls at one point come back faster than calls at new points, as in a fit.)

time_per_call <- function(f, reps = 50) {
  elapsed <- system.time(
    for (r in seq_len(reps)) {
      for (th in points) f(th)
    }
  )[["elapsed"]]
  1e6 * elapsed / (reps * length(points))
}
us <- rbind(
  logpost = c(
    R = time_per_call(function(th) logpost_r(th, Y)),
    RTMB = time_per_call(obj$fn),
    `C++` = time_per_call(function(th) logpost_cpp(th, Y))
  ),
  gradient = c(
    R = NA,
    RTMB = time_per_call(obj$gr),
    `C++` = time_per_call(function(th) grad_cpp(th, Y))
  ),
  hessian = c(R = NA, RTMB = time_per_call(hess_tape, reps = 1), `C++` = NA)
)
round(us, 1)
#>             R    RTMB C++
#> logpost  74.1   119.7 6.7
#> gradient   NA   195.8 7.2
#> hessian    NA 15430.0  NA

Replaying the tape takes 1.6 times as long as a call of logpost_r(), and RTMB’s gradient costs as much as 1.6 calls of its log-posterior. C++ is 11 times faster than R, and the hand-written gradient costs as much as 1.1 calls of its log-posterior. RTMB’s Hessian tape costs as much as 79 gradients, about one for each of the 39 parameters, and obj$he 40. The five fits, with the Hessian tape in the third:

fits <- list(
  R = inla_vanilla(logpost_r, init, Y = Y, silent = TRUE),
  RTMB = inla_vanilla(obj$fn, init, grad = obj$gr, silent = TRUE),
  `RTMB and Hessian` = inla_vanilla(
    obj$fn,
    init,
    grad = obj$gr,
    hess = hess_tape,
    silent = TRUE
  ),
  `C++` = inla_vanilla(logpost_cpp, init, Y = Y, silent = TRUE),
  `C++ and gradient` = inla_vanilla(
    logpost_cpp,
    init,
    grad = grad_cpp,
    Y = Y,
    silent = TRUE
  )
)
seconds <- vapply(fits, function(f) f$timing[["total"]], 0)
cbind(t(sapply(fits, function(f) f$counts)), seconds = round(seconds, 2))
#>                  logpost grad hess seconds
#> R                  13431    0    0    1.15
#> RTMB                1291  485    0    0.38
#> RTMB and Hessian     953  330   12    0.45
#> C++                13123    0    0    0.28
#> C++ and gradient    1288  483    0    0.14

Without a gradient the fit calls logpost 13,431 times. With one it calls logpost 1,291 times and the gradient 485 times. Without a gradient the count grows with the square of the number of parameters, and with one in proportion to it. Here a gradient saves time when it costs less than 25 calls of logpost. RTMB’s costs far less than that, and its fit is 3.1 times as fast as R’s. A hand-written gradient in C++ is the fastest of all.

Accuracy

Each fit against the one with the hand-written gradient: the skew-normal marginals (means, SDs and quantiles) and the VB mean in posterior SDs, and the log marginal likelihood in nats.

ref <- fits[["C++ and gradient"]]
sds <- ref$summary[, "SD"]
signif(
  t(sapply(fits, function(f) {
    c(
      marginals = max(abs(f$summary - ref$summary) / sds),
      vb_mean = max(abs(f$mean_vb - ref$mean_vb) / sds),
      logml = f$logml - ref$logml
    )
  })),
  2
)
#>                  marginals vb_mean   logml
#> R                  0.00300 0.03300 2.2e-02
#> RTMB               0.00011 0.00019 8.4e-05
#> RTMB and Hessian   0.00014 0.00023 1.0e-04
#> C++                0.00320 0.03300 2.2e-02
#> C++ and gradient   0.00000 0.00000 0.0e+00

RTMB’s fit is the hand-written gradient’s fit, since the two gradients agree to rounding error, and so is the fit with RTMB’s Hessian. The skew-normal marginals are nearly the same on every route: they are scanned around the mode and do not depend on the VB correction. Their differences, a few ten-thousandths of a posterior SD, come from the volume correction, a central difference with a gradient and a forward one otherwise. The gradient changes the VB correction, which then takes its step from the gradient at 2m + 1 = 79 points instead of from logpost at (m + 1)(m + 2) = 1,640 points (see the section on the VB correction in ?inla_vanilla). Here the fits without a gradient move the VB mean by up to 0.03 posterior SDs and the log marginal likelihood by 0.02. That is small, but it carries over to everything built on the VB mean: the log marginal likelihood, loo() and waic(), and the Gaussian marginals of marginals = "gaussian".

The Hessian

inla_vanilla() takes the Hessian as hess, after grad, as nlminb() does, and uses it in two places. nlminb() takes Newton steps to the mode. And the Hessian at the mode, which gives the covariance of the Laplace approximation, is RTMB’s rather than central differences of the gradient. The default marginals do not use it: their volume correction needs only two curvatures per parameter, and 4m + 1 = 157 gradients give them for every marginal at once, where a Hessian each would cost far more. The time each stage took, in seconds:

rtmb_fits <- fits[c("RTMB", "RTMB and Hessian")]
t(sapply(rtmb_fits, function(f) round(f$timing, 2)))
#>                  init laplace   vb marginals diagnostics total
#> RTMB             0.00    0.07 0.04      0.26           0  0.38
#> RTMB and Hessian 0.02    0.16 0.04      0.23           0  0.45

The marginals and the VB correction take the same time with and without it. The mode stage takes a little longer, because a Hessian costs about as much as m gradients, and the whole fit takes 1.21 times as long. The gap is smaller where the Hessian is sparse, as when each of many parameters enters only a few terms of the log-posterior: a Hessian tape then costs far fewer than m gradients.

The Hessian also finds the mode more precisely. nlminb() stops when its steps become small. The whitened gradient where it stopped in each fit is about how far it was from the mode, in posterior SDs:

signif(sapply(fits, function(f) f$diagnostics$optim$grad_mode), 1)
#>                R             RTMB RTMB and Hessian              C++ 
#>            2e-04            8e-05            4e-07            2e-04 
#> C++ and gradient 
#>            1e-04

Without the Hessian, nlminb() stops about a ten-thousandth of a posterior SD from the mode. With the Hessian it stops within a millionth. Either is far inside the check of the mode, which asks for a tenth. A supplied hess is itself checked at the mode against central differences of grad, with a warning if they do not match. With random effects integrated out, TMB gives no Hessian.

Using several cores

The skew-normal scans can run in parallel with cores, which needs the optional future package. With no random effects, as here, RTMB needs nothing special:

cores <- future::availableCores(omit = 1)
fit_par <- inla_vanilla(
  obj$fn, init, grad = obj$gr, width = "tk", cores = cores
)

Random effects are the exception. Forked workers, which cores uses in a terminal on macOS or Linux, share the tape. Separate R sessions, which it uses in RStudio, on Windows and in Positron, whose console refuses to fork, do not: once MakeADFun() integrates random effects out, a copy of obj$fn in another session returns NaN, with no error. The fit checks a worker’s value at the mode, finds the difference, and runs serially with a message.

To run in parallel there, we build the tape on each worker: the call of MakeADFun() goes in a function, which is called again when the process is not the one that started the fit.

build <- function() {
  RTMB::MakeADFun(model, parameters, random = "u", silent = TRUE)
}
obj <- build()
pid <- Sys.getpid()
rebuild <- function() {
  if (Sys.getpid() != pid) {
    obj <<- build()
    pid <<- Sys.getpid()
  }
}
logpost <- function(theta) {
  rebuild()
  -obj$fn(theta)
}
grad <- function(theta) {
  rebuild()
  -obj$gr(theta)
}
fit_par <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost, init, grad = grad, width = "tk", cores = cores
)

Whatever build() uses, here model and parameters, is found and sent to the workers. On a Poisson model with 21 parameters and 60 random intercepts integrated out, a fit with width = "tk" took 32 s serially and 4.4 s on 12 cores from a terminal. In Positron’s console it took 9.7 s: each worker is a new R session that has to start up, and the fit chose seven of the 12.

Choosing a route

In order of the work they take, with the first two about equal:

Route What you write Speed Accuracy
R logpost in R ✗ ✗
RTMB logpost in R, with RTMB’s functions, which give grad and hess ✓ ✓
Rcpp logpost in C++ ✓ ✗
R and a gradient logpost and its gradient in R ✗ ✓
Rcpp and a gradient logpost and its gradient in C++ ✓ ✓

Start with R. If RTMB has the functions your log-posterior needs, it gives the gradient’s accuracy for the same work, and the fit is 3.1 times as fast as R’s. A Hessian finds the mode more precisely for a little more time, so it is worth passing when it comes free, as from RTMB, but seldom worth deriving by hand. C++ buys speed, which matters when each call is expensive, as with a large data set, or when there are many, as with many parameters or many fits in a simulation study. A gradient by hand is the most work, since it has to be derived, checked and kept in step with the log-posterior, and only in C++ does it buy both.

References

Kristensen, K. (2026). RTMB: R bindings for TMB (Version 2.0) [Computer software]. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.RTMB

Kristensen, K., Nielsen, A., Berg, C. W., Skaug, H., & Bell, B. M. (2016). TMB: Automatic differentiation and Laplace approximation. Journal of Statistical Software, 70(5), 1–21. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v070.i05

Neudecker, H., & Satorra, A. (1991). Linear structural relations: Gradient and Hessian of the fitting function. Statistics & Probability Letters, 11(1), 57–61. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-7152(91)90178-T
